quick: Preferably on empty stomach, away from antacids/cations
Tendon/CNS symptoms, glucose, QT in at-risk
summary: Prulifloxacin is an oral broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone prodrug rapidly hydrolyzed to the active metabolite ulifloxacin. It is dosed 600 mg once daily for acute uncomplicated and complicated lower UTI and acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis. It carries the fluoroquinolone class risks of tendinopathy, QT prolongation, CNS effects, peripheral neuropathy and aortic aneurysm/dissection. Not FDA-approved; marketed in Europe (Unidrox), India and Japan.
indications: Acute uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) in adults
Complicated lower urinary tract infection in adults
Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis in adults

dosage.n: Up to 10 days depending on severity

admin: Take one 600 mg tablet orally once daily
Preferably on an empty stomach, at least 2 hours before or after meals
Separate from antacids, sucralfate, iron, calcium, magnesium, zinc and dairy by at least 2-4 hours to avoid chelation
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve
moa: Prulifloxacin is a prodrug rapidly metabolized by esterases to the active moiety ulifloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV. Inhibition of these enzymes blocks DNA replication, transcription, repair and recombination, leading to bactericidal activity against gram-negative and many gram-positive uropathogens and respiratory pathogens.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to prulifloxacin, ulifloxacin or other quinolones/fluoroquinolones
Children and growing adolescents (immature skeletal system)
History of tendon disorders related to quinolone administration
relative: Known QT prolongation or congenital long QT syndrome
Concurrent class IA/III antiarrhythmics or other QT-prolonging drugs
History of CNS disorders / seizure predisposition
monitor: Aortic aneurysm/dissection risk factors (elderly, hypertension, Marfan/Ehlers-Danlos)

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy. Fluoroquinolones may cause cartilage and joint damage in immature animals; adequate human data are lacking and use is not recommended.
lact: Contraindicated during breastfeeding. Quinolones are excreted in breast milk and pose a theoretical risk of cartilage toxicity to the infant; discontinue nursing or avoid the drug.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment. No formal dose adjustment is established for mild-to-moderate impairment, but use is not recommended in severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min) due to insufficient data. Ensure adequate hydration.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment. Activation of the prodrug to ulifloxacin may be affected; avoid in severe hepatic impairment owing to limited data.

major: QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, macrolides, tricyclics) - additive risk of torsades de pointes
Theophylline - quinolones may raise theophylline levels; monitor for toxicity
Tizanidine - increased levels with quinolones, hypotension and sedation
moderate: Multivalent cation products (antacids, iron, calcium, magnesium, zinc, sucralfate) - reduced absorption; separate dosing
Warfarin / vitamin K antagonists - enhanced anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
NSAIDs - may increase CNS stimulation and seizure risk
Oral hypoglycemic agents and insulin - dysglycemia (hypo- or hyperglycemia)
minor: Probenecid - reduced renal elimination of ulifloxacin
interactions.food: Dairy products and calcium/magnesium-rich foods reduce absorption; take apart from meals and cation-containing products.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; may potentiate CNS adverse effects such as dizziness and impaired alertness.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect glucose measurements; rarely elevates hepatic transaminases.

emergency: Aortic aneurysm rupture or dissection (sudden severe chest/back/abdominal pain)

monitoring: Tendon pain, swelling or inflammation - discontinue immediately if suspected
Symptoms of peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, weakness)
ECG/QT in patients with QT risk factors or electrolyte disturbance
Signs of CNS effects, including seizures or mood changes
counsel: Take one tablet once daily, preferably on an empty stomach, away from antacids, dairy, iron and calcium
Stop the drug and contact a clinician at once if tendon pain, swelling or rupture occurs
Report numbness, tingling, burning or weakness suggesting nerve damage
Avoid excessive sun and UV exposure; use sun protection (photosensitivity)
Seek urgent care for sudden severe chest, back or abdominal pain (aortic risk)
Avoid alcohol and use caution driving until effects are known
Complete the full course; report severe or bloody diarrhea
pk: Rapid absorption; active ulifloxacin formed within ~1 hour
Store below 30 C in original packaging, protect from moisture
pearls: Record sourced from EMA/SmPC and manufacturer prescribing information (e.g. Unidrox), not US FDA, as prulifloxacin is not FDA-approved
Prodrug rapidly converted by esterases to the active metabolite ulifloxacin
Once-daily 600 mg dosing simplifies short-course UTI therapy
Carries full fluoroquinolone class warnings: tendon rupture, neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation and aortic aneurysm/dissection
Separate from multivalent cations (antacids, iron, calcium, dairy) to preserve absorption
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the once-daily schedule; do not double the dose.
overdose: No specific antidote. Manage with supportive and symptomatic care, gastric emptying or activated charcoal if recent ingestion, adequate hydration and ECG monitoring for QT effects. Hemodialysis removes only a limited amount of ulifloxacin.
